A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core theory and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D support a reliable comparison, including relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C report original Transformer parity experiments and MLP identity-task experiments, including accuracy, loss, compression, and initialization comparisons.

after.justification: The original experimental studies remain, with revised numerical results and an additional Adam–SGD comparison in Appendix C.1, Table 3.

M1.justification: Sections 6.3 and B.12 add an alternative Transformer construction that encodes programs in MLP weights and first populates tape positions, instead of encoding programs in prefix embeddings. This extends the theoretical constructions; the principal GMM variational objective and experimentally evaluated architectures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate binary-sequence parity, including training lengths 1–20 and testing lengths 21–40, and a four-bit identity task. The new optimizer comparison uses the existing parity task. Alternative Transformer families receive theoretical discussion, not additional empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: V3 adds SGD as an evaluated alternative to Adam for optimizing the variational parity model in Appendix C.1, Table 3. The existing MLE baseline and manual-versus-random initialization comparisons remain. K-FAC is suggested for future work, not evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported MLP KL-coefficient sweep changes from 10^-1 through 10^-5 to 1 through 10^-4; the manual row changes from 10^-2 to 10^-1. V3 also adds the SGD optimizer comparison. These are reported setting changes, without evidence establishing whether the retained experiments were rerun; the other documented splits, architectures, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds an optimizer-sensitivity check comparing Adam and SGD, plus analytical component ablations showing how removing quantization, adaptive prefix length, and layerwise weight sharing weakens description-length bounds (Table 2 and Appendix B.11). Existing initialization comparisons, the MLP coefficient sweep, and the prior-collapse analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The documented Monte Carlo sampling procedures and sample counts for estimating the variational objective are unchanged.

E6.justification: Compression and loss values across both empirical tables are substantially revised. Table 1 changes random variational KL from 6.5M to 2.8M bits and manual KL from 2.0K to 870 bits, while preserving its accuracies. MLP baseline NLL changes from 20.3 to 8.82 bits, with other MLP results revised alongside changed coefficients. New Table 3 reports 49.6% OOD accuracy for SGD versus 60.4% for Adam. These are numerical revisions and added results, not established performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: V1 already derives the near-optimal bound using adaptive prefix length in Appendix B.11. V3 substantially extends that analysis with component-dependent bounds and an MLP-encoded construction having quadratic parameter scaling and linear rank (Sections 6.2–6.3 and B.11–B.12). Section 4.1 also removes the blanket identification of arbitrary program length with Kolmogorov complexity. The main existence theorems and their proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The fourth introductory contribution expands from empirical analysis of the variational objective to empirical and analytical study of multiple objectives, explicitly claiming bounds for alternative two-part codes. The abstract's central optimality, differentiability, and optimization-difficulty claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds explicit qualifications about additive constants and the limited functions constrained at finite resources. New discussion interprets SGD's underfitting through its KL–likelihood tradeoff and considers implications for prompt optimization, MLP compression, and decoder constructions. The original prior-collapse explanation and general optimization limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.12 and Figure 9 supply an ALTA program listing for the new tape-population construction and specify its Rt + Rs + 2 layer requirement. Experimental tables revise documented KL coefficients and identify the added SGD comparison. Most existing implementation, initialization, and training details are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations to Akinwande et al., Bornschein et al., Li and Wang, and Martens and Grosse. Their accompanying discussions connect the work to prompt optimization, prequential coding, decoder universality, and possible second-order optimization. The principal positioning relative to universal induction and neural compression remains stable.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the practical-considerations section and conclusion, organizes Section 6 into three subsections, and expands and retitles Appendix B.11. It also makes localized wording and typographical corrections and adds the conference header. Most existing exposition and appendix structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds the analytical-ablation table, optimizer-comparison table, and an ALTA code figure. Table 1 loses its total-codelength column, and the MLP table adopts grouped rows and scientific notation. Existing figures are visually retained; the original Figure 9 becomes Figure 10 and is repositioned.

improvement.justification: V3 improves the connection between the theoretical framework and practical code design through component-dependent bounds, an alternative construction, clearer finite-resource limitations, and an optimizer-sensitivity experiment. These are useful extensions while the central theory and empirical coverage remain stable. The unexplained numerical revisions and changed MLP coefficients do not themselves establish improved empirical performance, limiting the overall gain.
